extracted.intended_audience: students, naturalists, and anatomists interested in comparative primate anatomy/primatology
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and interpret anatomical characters used to compare and classify Man, the great apes (Gorilla, Chimpanzee, Orang), and lower apes/monkeys (Lemurs, Cebus, Marmosets, Baboons). Focuses on skeletal, dental, muscular, and cerebral features and how to weigh them comparatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vertebral counts and spinal curvature
rubrics_metrics.description: Number of dorsal and lumbar vertebrae (e.g., Gorilla sometimes 14 pairs; an Orang-Utan skeleton with 12 dorsal and 5 lumbar as in Man) and the degree/shape of spinal curves, especially lumbar convexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare both vertebral counts and the presence/absence/degree of spinal curves: Man shows marked lumbar convexity correlated with erect posture; young Gorilla and Chimpanzee preserved with ligaments display obvious curves, while young Orangs may have straight or even forward-concave lumbar regions. Note variability across apes—counts and curvature vary among lower apes, so use in combination with other characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pelvic (haunch) structure and relation to erect posture
rubrics_metrics.description: Shape and proportions of the pelvis: expanded haunch bones affording support for viscera in habitual erect posture; size and shape of the pelvic inlet and ischiatic prominences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human pelvis is adapted to upright posture (broad haunch bones, space for great muscles). Compare with Gorilla (considerable differences) and Gibbon (far more different from Gorilla than Gorilla from Man). In lower monkeys and lemurs the pelvis becomes quadrupedal. Pelvic features should be interpreted relative to locomotor habit and across taxa rather than in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skull proportions: face vs braincase, occipital foramen position, brow ridges/crests
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative predominance of the facial skeleton versus the cranial (brain) case; position of the occipital foramen on the skull base; development of supraciliary ridges (brow prominences) and cranial crests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gorilla: face (massive jaw-bones) predominates, occipital foramen lies in posterior third of base, large crests and overhanging brow ridges. Man: braincase predominates, foramen nearer center, smoother vault. Sections show some apparent defects in ape crania arise from excessive facial bone mass rather than malformed cranial cavity. Use internal casts/sections where possible to avoid misleading surface appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cranial capacity (absolute and relative) and its variability
rubrics_metrics.description: Volume of the cranial cavity (e.g., lowest adult human observed ~62–63 cubic inches; largest human ~114 cubic inches; most capacious Gorilla measured ~34.5 cubic inches; Gorilla range measured 24–34.5 cubic inches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret cranial capacity both absolutely and relatively: absolute differences between highest and lowest humans exceed that between lowest human and highest gorilla, while relative differences are of similar order. Expect considerable intraspecific variation (humans and gorillas vary substantially). Do not overvalue cranial capacity alone for taxonomic separation—compare ranges across series.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional size of facial bones and jaw projection (facial angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative size of facial bones and degree of jaw projection which determine the facial angle and perceived 'brutal' character of the skull.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large facial bones and strong jaw projection in Gorillas reduce facial angle and give a brutal aspect; other genera (e.g., Baboons) exaggerate muzzle proportions further. Evaluate proportional relationships (face vs braincase) rather than single measurements; compare across multiple genera to assess systematic value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occipital foramen position as a variable character
rubrics_metrics.description: Forward or posterior placement of the occipital foramen on the skull base varies between species (e.g., in Mycetes and some Lemurs it is far posterior; Chrysothrix may have it forward near Man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because position varies widely even within related groups, this character alone is unreliable for broad classificatory distinctions. Use it in combination with other cranial and postcranial characters and consider variation within genera.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dentition: tooth counts, diastema, canine size, molar form, and eruption order
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of milk and permanent dentition (Man: milk 20, permanent 32; Cebus/permanent 36 in some New World monkeys), presence/absence of diastema, relative canine size and projection, complexity of molar crowns and roots, and sequence of eruption (differences in timing between Man and Gorilla).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humans: regular even series without pronounced breaks. Gorillas exhibit diastema and large projecting canines; false molar roots more complex and molar proportions differ; eruption order differs (permanent canines appear after certain molars in Gorilla vs before in Man). New World monkeys (Cebus, marmosets) and lemurs show larger departures (tooth number and molar form). Use whole dentitional pattern for affinity judgments rather than single tooth differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hand vs foot diagnostic anatomical characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Defining features distinguishing a foot from a hand: (1) arrangement of the tarsal bones, (2) presence of a short flexor and a short extensor muscle of the digits, and (3) possession of the muscle termed 'peronaeus longus'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on proportions or mobility (e.g., an opposable great toe) to decide hand vs foot. Apply the three anatomical criteria listed to determine whether a terminal limb division is a hand or a foot. These characters are present in every monkey and lemur examined, even when proportions vary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carpal/tarsal bone arrangement and metapodial mobility
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed arrangement of carpal (wrist) and tarsal (ankle) bones and the relative mobility/articulation of metacarpals (thumb base) versus metatarsals (great toe base).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The human hand has two rows of carpal bones with specific metacarpal articulations; the foot differs by reduced tarsal number and different arrangement (e.g., calcaneum, astragalus, scaphoid). In Gorillas the foot resembles man's in number and disposition of tarsals but differs in proportions and mobility (more oblique set and more movable great-toe metatarsal). Use bone count and articulation patterns as diagnostic traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Muscle and tendon arrangement of digits (long vs short muscles; tendon interlacing)
rubrics_metrics.description: In hands, principal flexors and extensors are long muscles with fleshy parts in the arm and distinct tendons entering the hand; in feet some flexors/extensors are short (fleshy in sole or leg), tendons of long flexors may unite and commingle, and accessory fleshy bundles may be present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare presence/absence of short flexors/extensors, interlacing/unification of tendons, and accessory slips (e.g., in Gorilla one slip attached to tendons rather than heel bone). Variations in slips and tendon attachments increase in lower apes. These soft-tissue arrangements are diagnostic of functional differences and should be considered where soft-tissue or osteological correlates exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prehensility and mobility of the great toe vs thumb
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which the great toe is mobile/prehensile and approximates the thumb (opposability), noting that mobility varies with habit (e.g., uncivilized/barefoot populations show greater toe mobility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mobility/opposability of the great toe is variable and influenced by use; it is not a definitive anatomical test of hand vs foot. Interpret observations in light of the underlying skeletal and muscular characters (tarsal arrangement, short muscles, peronaeus longus).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative evaluation principle: weigh characters across the series
rubrics_metrics.description: For every constant difference between Man and the Gorilla a similar constant difference of the same order may be found between the Gorilla and some other ape; differences between Man and the highest Ape are often smaller than those between the highest and lower apes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat single differences as decisive; assess characters across a broad comparative series (Man, great apes, lower apes, New World monkeys, Lemurs). The systematic value of a character must be judged by its distribution and degree of change across the series, not merely by contrast with Man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presence and significance of the corpus callosum ('great commissure')
rubrics_metrics.description: Appearance of the great commissure (corpus callosum) in placental mammals marks a major structural change connecting the cerebral hemispheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If current statements hold, the corpus callosum represents one of the greatest and most sudden brain modifications in vertebrates. Its presence is a major dividing line in cerebral organization and should be noted in comparative assessments of brain evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Posterior lobe / posterior cornu / hippocampus minor development
rubrics_metrics.description: Development of the posterior lobe of the cerebral hemisphere which overlaps/hides the cerebellum and contains a posterior cornu of the lateral ventricle and an associated hippocampus minor (a sulcus/eminence beneath the cornu floor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher placental mammals, old- and new-world monkeys, and man-like apes possess a well-developed posterior lobe, posterior cornu, and hippocampus minor; lemurs show these structures rudimentary and cerebellum partially visible from above. Use the degree of posterior lobe and hippocampus minor development as strong phylogenetic indicators, keeping in mind gradations across taxa.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cerebral surface convolution complexity (sulci and convolutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree of sulcation/convolution of the cerebral hemispheres: from smooth or few sulci in lower mammals to highly convoluted surfaces in larger/higher orders (Elephant, Porpoise, higher Apes, Man).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convolution complexity increases with cerebral development and is particularly pronounced in large-brained mammals and primates. Evaluate relative convolution patterns and number of sulci as part of overall brain morphology comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ventricular morphology: anterior, descending, and posterior cornu presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure of the cerebral ventricles within hemispheres including anterior cornu, descending cornu, and where present a posterior cornu extending into the posterior lobe.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the posterior lobe is developed a posterior cornu commonly appears; the ventricular morphology (presence/size/extent of horns) correlates with external lobe development and should be consulted (via internal casts or sections) for assessing cerebral differences.
